PSE II · Chapter 28

Magnetic Fields

Forces on moving charge & their sources

← PSE II Course

28.0 — A Force That Steers

Every force in this course so far has pushed along a line: gravity and the electric force point along the line between two objects, and a spring pushes along its own length. The magnetic force breaks the pattern. It acts on a charge only while the charge is moving, and it pushes sideways, at right angles to the motion. It steers a charge without ever speeding it up or slowing it down.

The compass came first. Shen Kuo (1031–1095) described the magnetic needle and its use in navigation in 1088. The link to electricity waited until 1820, when Hans Christian Ørsted (1777–1851) saw a compass needle swing beside a wire carrying current during a lecture. Within months Jean-Baptiste Biot and Félix Savart had measured the field around a wire, and André-Marie Ampère had shown that two wires carrying current push or pull on each other.

“From the preceding facts we may likewise infer that this conflict performs circles … it is the nature of a circle that the motions in opposite parts should have an opposite direction.” — Hans Christian Ørsted, Experiments on the Effect of a Current of Electricity on the Magnetic Needle, 1820

Chapter 31 used the magnetic field mostly as the partner that keeps a light wave moving, and it borrowed two facts about it: \(\vec B\) is a vector field, and it has a flux. This chapter takes \(\vec B\) on its own terms in two halves. §28.1–28.4 ask what a given field does to a moving charge, a wire and a loop. §28.5–28.7 ask where a field comes from, which is the static half of Chapter 31’s law (4), and they end with the force between two currents that fixes the value of \(\mu_0\).

*Personal note: Ørsted’s discovery is usually told as an accident. It was an accident only in its timing; he had been looking for a link between electricity and magnetism for years, and he knew what he was seeing when the needle moved.

28.1 — The Magnetic Field

Measuring a Field That Ignores Charges at Rest

Chapter 22 defined \(\vec E\) by holding a test charge still and measuring the force on it: \(\vec E = \vec F/q\). Near a magnet that test fails. A charge at rest feels no magnetic force at all. The magnetic field has to be measured with a moving charge, and firing test charges through a region in different directions turns up three facts:

  1. There is one direction (and its reverse) along which a moving charge feels no force. That line is the direction of \(\vec B\).
  2. Moving at an angle \(\theta\) to that line, the charge feels a force proportional to \(|q|\), to \(v\), and to \(\sin\theta\), largest at \(\theta = 90°\).
  3. The force is always perpendicular both to the velocity and to the field’s line.

The magnitude of the field is the largest force per unit charge per unit speed, \(B = F_\text{max}/(|q|v)\). Its SI unit is the tesla (T); from the definition,

\[1\ \text{T} = 1\ \frac{\text{N}}{\text{C}\cdot\text{m/s}} = 1\ \frac{\text{N}}{\text{A}\cdot\text{m}}\]

Source Approximate \(B\)
Earth’s surface \(50\ \mu\text{T}\)
Refrigerator magnet, at its face \(5\ \text{mT}\)
MRI scanner \(1.5\)–\(3\ \text{T}\)
Strongest steady laboratory magnets \(\sim 45\ \text{T}\)

A tesla is a large field. An MRI magnet is tens of thousands of times stronger than Earth’s field, which is still enough to turn a compass needle.

Electric Field and Magnetic Field

Property Electric field \(\vec E\) (Ch 22) Magnetic field \(\vec B\) (this chapter)
Made by any charge moving charge: currents and magnets
Force on a charge \(\vec F = q\vec E\), along \(\vec E\) \(\vec F = q\vec v\times\vec B\), perpendicular to \(\vec v\) and \(\vec B\) (§28.2)
Force on a charge at rest? yes no
Does work on the charge? yes no (§28.2)
Field lines begin on \(+\), end on \(-\) close on themselves
Flux out of a closed surface \(Q_\text{enc}/\varepsilon_0\) (Ch 23) always \(0\) (§28.7)

The last row is the deepest difference. Electric field lines start and stop on charges. Magnetic field lines never stop, because there is no magnetic charge for them to stop on. §28.7 writes that fact as Chapter 31’s law (2).

28.2 — The Force on a Moving Charge

The Force Law

The three measurements of §28.1 are summarized by one vector product, the magnetic part of the Lorentz force:

\[\boxed{\;\vec F = q\,\vec v\times\vec B, \qquad F = |q|\,vB\sin\theta\;}\]

This is a law read from experiment, not derived; the cross product is the mathematical object that has exactly the three properties measured. (The full Lorentz force adds the electric part: \(\vec F = q\vec E + q\vec v\times\vec B\).)

Direction. Point the fingers of the right hand along \(\vec v\) and curl them toward \(\vec B\); the thumb gives \(\vec v\times\vec B\). That is the force on a positive charge. For a negative charge, \(q < 0\) flips the vector: the force is opposite the thumb. An electron and a proton fired the same way through the same field are pushed in opposite directions (Figure 28.2).

Check the force law.

  • Charge at rest. \(v = 0\) gives \(F = 0\), as measured.
  • Along the field. \(\theta = 0°\) or \(180°\) gives \(\sin\theta = 0\), so \(F = 0\): a charge moving along \(\vec B\) is untouched.
  • No work. \(\vec F\) is perpendicular to \(\vec v\) at every instant, so the power \(\vec F\cdot\vec v\) is zero and so is the work. A magnetic force never changes a charge’s speed or kinetic energy; it changes only the direction of motion.

Circular Orbits

Take a charge moving perpendicular to a uniform field. The force has constant size \(|q|vB\) (the speed never changes) and always points at right angles to the velocity, which is exactly the condition for uniform circular motion (Figure 28.3).

Step 1 — the force is the centripetal force.

\[|q|vB = \frac{mv^2}{r}\]

Step 2 — solve for the radius.

\[r = \frac{mv}{|q|B}\]

Step 3 — the time for one orbit. One lap is \(2\pi r\) at speed \(v\):

\[T = \frac{2\pi r}{v} = \frac{2\pi m}{|q|B}\]

\[\boxed{\;r = \frac{mv}{|q|B}, \qquad T = \frac{2\pi m}{|q|B}, \qquad f = \frac{1}{T} = \frac{|q|B}{2\pi m}\;}\]

Check the limits.

  • Stronger field, tighter circle. \(r \propto 1/B\); as \(B \to 0\), \(r \to \infty\) and the path straightens out.
  • Faster charge, wider circle. \(r \propto v\).
  • The period does not depend on the speed. A faster charge travels a larger circle in exactly the same time. This is why a cyclotron works: all particles with the same \(q/m\) come around in step, so one oscillating voltage can push each of them once per lap.

A velocity with a component along \(\vec B\). Split \(\vec v\) into a part along \(\vec B\) and a part across it. The part along \(\vec B\) feels no force (the check above), so it carries on unchanged, while the part across \(\vec B\) drives the circle. Together they make a helix. Charged particles from the Sun spiral this way along Earth’s field lines into the polar atmosphere, and the aurora is where they hit.

Example: From an Accelerating Voltage to an Orbit

A proton starts from rest, is accelerated through a potential difference \(\Delta V\), and enters a uniform field \(B\) at right angles. Find its speed, the radius of its orbit and its period. Then find the radius for an electron accelerated through the same \(\Delta V\). Use \(\Delta V = 2.00\) kV and \(B = 0.100\) T.

Why it matters: the voltage and the field are the two knobs on the bench; the radius is where the beam lands. Every mass spectrometer and particle beamline is designed from this chain.

Step 1 — speed from energy (Chapter 24). The field does work \(q\Delta V\) on the charge, all of it kinetic energy:

\[|q|\Delta V = \tfrac12 mv^2 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad v = \sqrt{\frac{2|q|\Delta V}{m}}\]

Step 2 — radius and period.

\[r = \frac{mv}{|q|B} = \frac{1}{B}\sqrt{\frac{2m\Delta V}{|q|}}, \qquad T = \frac{2\pi m}{|q|B}\]

At the same \(\Delta V\) and \(B\), \(r \propto \sqrt{m/|q|}\).

Step 3 — numbers. \(m_p = 1.67\times10^{-27}\) kg, \(e = 1.60\times10^{-19}\) C, \(m_e = 9.11\times10^{-31}\) kg:

\[\boxed{\;v = \sqrt{\frac{2(1.60\times10^{-19})(2.00\times10^{3})}{1.67\times10^{-27}}} = 6.19\times10^{5}\ \text{m/s}, \qquad r = \frac{(1.67\times10^{-27})(6.19\times10^{5})}{(1.60\times10^{-19})(0.100)} = 6.46\ \text{cm}\;}\] \[\boxed{\;T = \frac{2\pi(1.67\times10^{-27})}{(1.60\times10^{-19})(0.100)} = 0.656\ \mu\text{s}, \qquad r_e = r\sqrt{\frac{m_e}{m_p}} = (6.46\ \text{cm})(0.0234) = 1.51\ \text{mm}\;}\]

The electron, about 1800 times lighter, curls in a circle 43 times smaller, and the opposite way round, because its charge is negative. Doubling \(\Delta V\) would widen the proton’s circle by \(\sqrt2\) and leave its period unchanged.

Crossed Fields: Selecting One Speed

Put a uniform \(\vec E\) and a uniform \(\vec B\) at right angles to each other and to a beam (Figure 28.4, left). For a positive charge moving right, with \(\vec E\) down and \(\vec B\) into the page, the electric force \(q\vec E\) points down and the magnetic force \(q\vec v\times\vec B\) points up.

Step 1 — balance the two forces.

\[qE = qvB\]

Step 2 — solve for the speed. The charge, the mass and even the sign cancel:

\[\boxed{\;v = \frac{E}{B}\;}\]

Only particles at this one speed go straight through. A faster one feels the larger magnetic force and is bent one way; a slower one is bent the other way. The device is a velocity selector, a filter that hands the next stage a beam of one known speed.

The same balance inside a conductor is the Hall effect. In a strip carrying current across a field, the magnetic force pushes the moving carriers toward one edge. Charge piles up there until its electric field \(E_H\) balances the magnetic push, \(qE_H = qv_dB\). The voltage across a strip of width \(w\) is then \(V_H = E_Hw = v_dBw\), proportional to \(B\), which is how a Hall probe (and the compass in a phone) measures a magnetic field.

Example: A Mass Spectrometer

Singly ionized carbon atoms, \(^{12}\)C\(^+\) and \(^{13}\)C\(^+\), leave a velocity selector with \(E = 8.00\times10^4\) V/m and \(B_1 = 0.320\) T. They pass through a slit into a region of field \(B_2 = 0.300\) T alone, travel half a circle, and land on a detector (Figure 28.4). Find where each isotope lands, measured from the slit. Use \(1\ \text{u} = 1.66\times10^{-27}\) kg.

Why it matters: the landing spot is what you can see; the mass is what you want. This is how isotope ratios are counted for carbon dating, and how a drug or a pollutant is identified from its molecules.

Step 1 — the speed. From the selector, \(v = E/B_1\), the same for both isotopes.

Step 2 — the landing distance. A half circle puts the ion down at the far end of a diameter:

\[x = 2r = \frac{2mv}{qB_2} = \frac{2mE}{qB_1B_2}\]

With \(v\) fixed, \(x \propto m\): the landing spot is a direct reading of the mass.

Step 3 — numbers. \(v = (8.00\times10^4)/(0.320) = 2.50\times10^5\) m/s; \(m_{12} = 12(1.66\times10^{-27}) = 1.992\times10^{-26}\) kg and \(m_{13} = 2.158\times10^{-26}\) kg:

\[\boxed{\;x_{12} = \frac{2(1.992\times10^{-26})(2.50\times10^{5})}{(1.60\times10^{-19})(0.300)} = 20.8\ \text{cm}, \qquad x_{13} = \frac{2(2.158\times10^{-26})(2.50\times10^{5})}{(1.60\times10^{-19})(0.300)} = 22.5\ \text{cm}\;}\]

The two isotopes land \(1.7\) cm apart, easily resolved. One mass unit shifts the landing spot by \(1.7\) cm everywhere on this detector, because \(x\) is linear in \(m\).

28.3 — The Force on a Wire

From One Charge to a Current

A wire carrying current in a magnetic field is pushed sideways, because every moving carrier inside it is. Add up the forces on all of them.

Step 1 — count the carriers. A straight segment of length \(L\) and cross-section \(A\), with \(n\) carriers per unit volume, holds \(nAL\) carriers, each of charge \(q\) drifting at \(\vec v_d\).

Step 2 — add their forces. Each feels \(q\vec v_d\times\vec B\), all in the same direction:

\[\vec F = (nAL)\,q\,\vec v_d\times\vec B\]

Step 3 — recognize the current (Chapter 26). \(nqv_dA = I\). Let \(\vec L\) be a vector of length \(L\) along the current:

\[\boxed{\;\vec F = I\vec L\times\vec B, \qquad F = ILB\sin\theta\;}\]

Nothing new has been assumed: this is \(q\vec v\times\vec B\) summed over about \(10^{23}\) carriers. The right-hand rule now runs with the fingers along the current. For a wire bent into a curve, the same result holds for each short piece, \(d\vec F = I\,d\vec\ell\times\vec B\). For a coil of \(N\) turns, \(N\) segments of length \(L\) lie side by side carrying the same current, so the force on that side of the coil is \(N\) times as large: \(F = NILB\).

Check the limits.

  • Wire along the field. \(\theta = 0\) gives \(F = 0\).
  • Reverse the current. \(\vec L \to -\vec L\) reverses the force. A wire in a field carrying alternating current shakes back and forth, which is how a loudspeaker cone is driven.
  • Sign of the carriers. Electrons drift opposite to \(I\) with \(q < 0\); the two sign flips cancel, so the force depends only on the direction of \(I\).

Example: Weighing a Magnetic Field

A current balance hangs a rectangular coil of \(N\) turns from one arm of a balance. Only the bottom side of the coil, of length \(L\), sits in the uniform field to be measured, which points into the page (Figure 28.6). With no current the balance is level. With current \(I\) the bottom side is pulled down, and a mass \(m\) added to the other pan restores the balance. Find \(B\) for \(N = 20\), \(L = 4.00\) cm, \(I = 1.50\) A and \(m = 2.45\) g.

Why it matters: a ruler, an ammeter and a known mass give the field, with no field meter needed. Run backward (a known field, a measured current), the same balance is how the kilogram has been realized since 2019, in the Kibble balance.

Step 1 — which forces matter. The two vertical sides carry current in opposite directions, so their forces are equal and opposite and cancel. The top side is outside the field. Only the bottom side counts: \(N\) segments of length \(L\), current across the field, force \(NILB\) straight down.

Step 2 — balance. The arms are equal, so the added weight equals the magnetic force:

\[NILB = mg \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad B = \frac{mg}{NIL}\]

Step 3 — numbers.

\[\boxed{\;B = \frac{(2.45\times10^{-3}\ \text{kg})(9.80\ \text{m/s}^2)}{(20)(1.50\ \text{A})(0.0400\ \text{m})} = \frac{0.0240\ \text{N}}{1.20\ \text{A}\cdot\text{m}} = 0.0200\ \text{T} = 20.0\ \text{mT}\;}\]

The force being weighed is \(0.024\) N, the weight of a small paper clip. The 20 turns multiply it twentyfold; with a single turn the balance would need \(0.12\) g, hard to measure.

28.4 — Torque on a Current Loop

Four Sides, Two Forces, One Torque

Bend the wire into a rectangular loop, sides \(a\) and \(b\), carrying current \(I\) in a uniform field. The loop is free to turn about an axis through its center, parallel to the sides of length \(b\) and perpendicular to \(\vec B\). Let \(\hat n\) be the loop’s normal, given by the right-hand rule (curl the fingers with the current, thumb along \(\hat n\)), at angle \(\theta\) to \(\vec B\) (Figure 28.7).

Step 1 — the two sides of length \(a\). Their currents are opposite, so their forces are equal and opposite, and both lie along the axis, on the same line. They cancel and produce no torque.

Step 2 — the two sides of length \(b\). Each is perpendicular to \(\vec B\), so each feels \(F = IbB\). The currents are opposite, so the forces are opposite: zero net force, but they act on opposite sides of the axis.

Step 3 — the moment arm. Each side of length \(b\) is a distance \(a/2\) from the axis. The forces are perpendicular to \(\vec B\), and the line from the axis to each side is perpendicular to \(\hat n\), so the moment arm of each force is \((a/2)\sin\theta\).

Step 4 — add the two torques. They turn the loop the same way:

\[\tau = 2\,(IbB)\left(\frac{a}{2}\sin\theta\right) = IabB\sin\theta = IAB\sin\theta\]

with \(A = ab\) the loop’s area. \(N\) turns multiply it by \(N\).

The Magnetic Dipole Moment

Everything about the loop that matters enters as one vector, the magnetic dipole moment, \(\vec\mu = NIA\,\hat n\) (unit A·m²). In terms of it the torque is a cross product. The energy follows as it did for the electric dipole in Chapter 25. The torque \(\mu B\sin\theta\) always turns \(\hat n\) toward \(\vec B\), so as the loop turns from \(\theta = 90°\) (chosen as \(U = 0\)) to \(\theta\), the field does work \(W = \int_{90°}^{\theta}(-\mu B\sin\theta')\,d\theta' = \mu B\cos\theta\), and \(U = -W\):

\[\boxed{\;\vec\mu = NIA\,\hat n, \qquad \vec\tau = \vec\mu\times\vec B, \qquad U = -\vec\mu\cdot\vec B = -\mu B\cos\theta\;}\]

Chapter 25 promised this. The electric dipole \(\vec p = q\vec d\) in a field \(\vec E\) had \(\vec\tau = \vec p\times\vec E\) and \(U = -\vec p\cdot\vec E\). Same mathematics, different letters:

Electric dipole (Ch 25) Magnetic dipole (this chapter)
Moment \(\vec p = q\vec d\) \(\vec\mu = NIA\,\hat n\)
Torque \(\vec\tau = \vec p\times\vec E\) \(\vec\tau = \vec\mu\times\vec B\)
Energy \(U = -\vec p\cdot\vec E\) \(U = -\vec\mu\cdot\vec B\)
Stable \(\vec p\) along \(\vec E\) \(\vec\mu\) along \(\vec B\)

Check the limits.

  • \(\hat n\) along \(\vec B\) (\(\theta = 0\)): \(\tau = 0\) and \(U = -\mu B\) is a minimum. The loop rests there, like a compass needle pointing north.
  • \(\hat n\) opposite \(\vec B\) (\(\theta = 180°\)): \(\tau = 0\) again, but \(U\) is a maximum, an unstable balance.
  • \(\theta = 90°\): the torque is largest, \(\tau = NIAB\).

A DC motor is this loop on an axle. Left alone it would swing to \(\theta = 0\) and stop; a split-ring commutator reverses the current every half turn, so the torque keeps pointing the same way round and the loop keeps turning. A bar magnet behaves like a loop because each of its atoms carries a tiny magnetic moment, and in a magnet they are lined up.

Example: The Galvanometer

An analog meter’s movement is a coil of \(N\) turns and area \(A\) that turns between curved pole pieces around a fixed iron core (Figure 28.8). The curved gap makes the field point radially, so wherever the coil turns, its plane lies along \(\vec B\) and \(\theta = 90°\). A hairspring resists with torque \(\kappa\phi\) at deflection \(\phi\). Find the deflection for a current \(I\), and the current that swings the needle a full \(90°\), for \(N = 100\), a coil \(2.00\) cm by \(1.50\) cm, \(B = 0.200\) T and \(\kappa = 2.00\times10^{-7}\) N·m/rad.

Why it matters: the needle angle is what you read; the current is what you want. This is the movement inside the analog ammeters and voltmeters of Chapter 27, which are a galvanometer with a resistor in parallel or in series.

Step 1 — balance the torques. With \(\theta = 90°\) at every angle,

\[NIAB = \kappa\phi \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \phi = \frac{NAB}{\kappa}\,I\]

The deflection is proportional to the current, so the scale is evenly spaced. That is what the radial field buys; in a uniform field the torque would fall off as \(\sin\theta\) and the scale would crowd at one end.

Step 2 — full scale. \(\phi = 90.0° = \pi/2\) rad and \(A = (0.0200)(0.0150) = 3.00\times10^{-4}\) m²:

\[\boxed{\;I_\text{fs} = \frac{\kappa\phi}{NAB} = \frac{(2.00\times10^{-7})(\pi/2)}{(100)(3.00\times10^{-4})(0.200)} = \frac{3.14\times10^{-7}}{6.00\times10^{-3}} = 5.24\times10^{-5}\ \text{A} = 52.4\ \mu\text{A}\;}\]

A movement this sensitive reads at most about \(50\ \mu\)A. To read 5 A as an ammeter, Chapter 27’s shunt resistor carries all but one part in \(10^5\) of the current around it.

28.5 — Sources of the Field: The Biot–Savart Law

The Magnetic Coulomb’s Law

§28.2–28.4 took the field as given. Ørsted’s needle says currents make it. Biot and Savart measured the field of each short piece of a current, and the result has the shape of Coulomb’s law for a piece of charge (Chapter 22). A current element \(I\,d\vec\ell\) makes, at a point a distance \(r\) away in the direction \(\hat r\),

\[\boxed{\;d\vec B = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\,\frac{I\,d\vec\ell\times\hat r}{r^2}\;}\]

where \(\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \text{T}\cdot\text{m/A}\) is the permeability of free space from Chapter 31. Like Coulomb’s law, it is read from experiment, and the total field is the sum \(\vec B = \int d\vec B\) over the whole current.

Coulomb (Ch 22) Biot–Savart (this chapter)
Source charge \(dq\) current element \(I\,d\vec\ell\)
Field \(d\vec E = k\,\dfrac{dq}{r^2}\,\hat r\) \(d\vec B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\,\dfrac{I\,d\vec\ell\times\hat r}{r^2}\)
Falls off as \(1/r^2\) \(1/r^2\)
Direction along \(\hat r\), away from the source perpendicular to both \(d\vec\ell\) and \(\hat r\)

The last row is why \(\vec E\) points away from a charge while \(\vec B\) circles a current.

The Field of a Long Straight Wire

The calculation is the one Chapter 22 used for the field beside a charged rod, with the cross product in place of the components.

Step 1 — set up. Put the wire along the \(y\)-axis carrying \(I\) upward, and the field point \(P\) a distance \(a\) to its right (Figure 28.9b). An element \(dy\) at height \(y\) is a distance \(r = \sqrt{y^2 + a^2}\) from \(P\).

Step 2 — direction. For every element, \(d\vec\ell\times\hat r\) points the same way, into the page at \(P\), so the magnitudes simply add.

Step 3 — magnitude of one piece. \(|d\vec\ell\times\hat r| = dy\,\sin\phi\), where \(\phi\) is the angle between the wire and \(\hat r\), and \(\sin\phi = a/r\):

\[dB = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi}\,\frac{a\,dy}{(y^2 + a^2)^{3/2}}\]

Step 4 — integrate over the whole wire. With \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} dy/(y^2 + a^2)^{3/2} = 2/a^2\) (the same table integral as the charged rod),

\[B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi}\,a\cdot\frac{2}{a^2}\]

\[\boxed{\;B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}\;}\]

writing \(r\) again for the distance from the wire. Direction: the field lines are circles around the wire. Point the right thumb along the current and the fingers curl the way \(\vec B\) goes (Figure 28.9a).

Check the result.

  • Far away. \(B \to 0\) as \(r \to \infty\), but only as \(1/r\), slower than a point source’s \(1/r^2\). It matches the infinite line of charge, \(E = \lambda/2\pi\varepsilon_0 r\) (Chapter 23): a long source falls off more slowly because there is always more of it nearby.
  • More current, more field. \(B \propto I\).
  • Units. \(\text{T}\cdot\text{m/A}\times\text{A}/\text{m} = \text{T}\).

The Field at the Center of a Loop

A loop of radius \(R\) is the easiest Biot–Savart sum of all, because every element is in the same position relative to the center (Figure 28.10).

Step 1 — geometry. Every element is a distance \(R\) from the center, and every \(d\vec\ell\) is perpendicular to the \(\hat r\) pointing at the center, so \(|d\vec\ell\times\hat r| = d\ell\).

Step 2 — direction. Every element’s field at the center points the same way, along the loop’s axis (the right-hand rule: fingers with the current, thumb along \(\vec B\) at the center).

Step 3 — add. The pieces add straight up to the loop’s length \(2\pi R\):

\[B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi R^2}\oint d\ell = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi R^2}(2\pi R)\]

\[\boxed{\;B_\text{center} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2R} \qquad (N \text{ turns: } N\mu_0I/2R)\;}\]

Far from the loop along its axis the field falls off as \(1/x^3\), the same as the electric field far from an electric dipole (Chapter 22); this is stated, not derived here. A current loop is a magnetic dipole, the source of the \(\vec\mu\) of §28.4.

Example: A Coil and a Wire

(a) A flat coil of \(N\) turns and radius \(R\) carries current \(I\). Find the field at its center for \(N = 50\), \(R = 10.0\) cm, \(I = 2.00\) A, and compare it with Earth’s field. (b) Find the field \(10.0\) cm from a long wire carrying \(5.00\) A.

Why it matters: the current, the turns and the radius are all set on the bench; the field at the center is what the coil delivers. A pair of coils like this is how a laboratory makes a known field, or cancels Earth’s.

Step 1 — symbols.

\[B_\text{coil} = \frac{N\mu_0 I}{2R}, \qquad B_\text{wire} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}\]

Step 2 — numbers.

\[\boxed{\;B_\text{coil} = \frac{(50)(4\pi\times10^{-7})(2.00)}{2(0.100)} = 0.628\ \text{mT} \approx 13\,B_\text{Earth}, \qquad B_\text{wire} = \frac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(5.00)}{2\pi(0.100)} = 10.0\ \mu\text{T}\;}\]

The modest coil overwhelms Earth’s \(50\ \mu\)T at its center. The wire’s field is a fifth of Earth’s at 10 cm and would equal it at 2 cm; this is why a compass held near a wire carrying a few amperes swings.

Two Wires: Superposition and the Force Between Currents

Magnetic fields add as vectors, just as electric fields did (Chapter 22). Two long parallel wires a distance \(d\) apart, with currents \(I_1\) and \(I_2\), each make the circular field of a single wire, and the field at any point is the vector sum. Run the right-hand rule once for each wire, then add (Figure 28.11a).

Each wire also sits in the other’s field and carries current across it, so each feels a force. Look at wire 2.

Step 1 — the field wire 1 makes at wire 2. A distance \(d\) away,

\[B_1 = \frac{\mu_0 I_1}{2\pi d}\]

perpendicular to the plane of the wires.

Step 2 — the force on a length \(L\) of wire 2 (§28.3). The current \(I_2\) runs perpendicular to \(\vec B_1\):

\[F_{\text{on }2} = I_2LB_1 = \frac{\mu_0 I_1I_2L}{2\pi d}\]

Step 3 — direction. Both currents out of the page: wire 1’s field at wire 2 (on its right) points up the page, and \(I_2\vec L\times\vec B_1\) = (out) × (up) points toward wire 1. Parallel currents attract. Reverse \(I_2\) and the force reverses: antiparallel currents repel (Figure 28.11b).

Step 4 — the force on wire 1. Run the same steps with the labels swapped: \(F_{\text{on }1} = I_1LB_2 = I_1L\,\mu_0I_2/(2\pi d)\), the same size, pointing toward wire 2.

\[\boxed{\;\frac{F}{L} = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d} \qquad \text{parallel currents attract, antiparallel repel}\;}\]

Check the result.

  • Newton’s third law, even with unequal currents. The formula is symmetric in \(I_1\) and \(I_2\): the force on wire 1 equals the force on wire 2 in size and is opposite in direction, however different the currents. A wire carrying ten times the current does not pull ten times harder; it makes ten times the field, which acts on the other wire’s smaller current.
  • One current turned off. As \(I_2 \to 0\), both forces go to zero together. Wire 1’s field at wire 2, \(\mu_0I_1/2\pi d\), does not change; there is simply no current in wire 2 for it to push on.
  • Far apart. \(d \to \infty\) gives \(F \to 0\), falling as \(1/d\).

This is where \(\mu_0\) comes from. Until 2019 the ampere was defined by this force: one ampere is the current that, in two long parallel wires one meter apart, gives a force of exactly \(2\times10^{-7}\) N per meter of wire. Put \(I_1 = I_2 = 1\) A and \(d = 1\) m into the result and it says \(\mu_0/2\pi = 2\times10^{-7}\), so \(\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\) T·m/A exactly. That is the “force between currents” Chapter 31 credited for the speed of light. (Since 2019 the ampere is fixed through the electron’s charge instead, and \(\mu_0\) is measured; it still agrees with \(4\pi\times10^{-7}\) to one part in \(10^{10}\).)

Example: Two Wires Carrying Opposite Currents

Two long parallel wires \(d\) apart carry \(I_1\) and \(I_2\) in opposite directions. Find the field at the midpoint and the force per unit length on each wire, for \(d = 10.0\) cm, \(I_1 = 3.00\) A and \(I_2 = 5.00\) A.

Why it matters: the currents and the spacing are set; the field between the wires and the force on them are what the design has to live with. In a power substation the busbars carry about 20 kA, 10 cm apart. The formula gives \(800\) N on every meter during a short circuit, and that is why the bars are bolted down.

Step 1 — the field at the midpoint. Each wire is \(d/2\) away. Seen end on, with \(I_1\) out of the page on the left and \(I_2\) into the page on the right, the right-hand rule gives both fields pointing up the page between the wires (Figure 28.11a), so the magnitudes add:

\[B_\text{mid} = \frac{\mu_0 I_1}{2\pi(d/2)} + \frac{\mu_0 I_2}{2\pi(d/2)} = \frac{\mu_0(I_1 + I_2)}{\pi d}\]

Step 2 — the force. From the result above, opposite currents repel:

\[\frac{F}{L} = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d}\]

Step 3 — numbers.

\[\boxed{\;B_\text{mid} = \frac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(3.00 + 5.00)}{\pi(0.100)} = 32.0\ \mu\text{T, up the page}\;}\] \[\boxed{\;\frac{F}{L} = \frac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(3.00)(5.00)}{2\pi(0.100)} = 3.00\times10^{-5}\ \text{N/m, pushing the wires apart}\;}\]

The two wires feel the same \(30\ \mu\)N per meter, although one carries two-thirds more current than the other. With parallel currents the fields at the midpoint would oppose, giving \(8.0\ \mu\)T, and the wires would attract.

28.6 — Ampère’s Law

The Shortcut, from Chapter 31

Chapter 31 stated law (4), the Ampère–Maxwell law:

\[\oint\vec B\cdot d\vec\ell = \mu_0 I_\text{enc} + \mu_0\varepsilon_0\frac{d\Phi_E}{dt}\]

For steady currents nothing is changing, so the second term is zero and what remains is Ampère’s law:

\[\boxed{\;\oint\vec B\cdot d\vec\ell = \mu_0 I_\text{enc}\;}\]

The circulation of \(\vec B\) around any closed loop equals \(\mu_0\) times the current through the loop. It plays the part Gauss’s law played for \(\vec E\) in Chapter 23: always true, and useful only when symmetry makes \(B\) constant along a loop we can draw.

Gauss’s law (Ch 23) Ampère’s law (this chapter)
Measures flux out of a closed surface circulation around a closed loop
Counts charge enclosed, \(Q_\text{enc}\) current through, \(I_\text{enc}\)
Constant \(1/\varepsilon_0\) \(\mu_0\)
Useful when \(E\) is constant over the surface \(B\) is constant along the loop

The long wire again. Take a circle of radius \(r\) around the wire. By symmetry \(\vec B\) runs along the circle with the same size everywhere on it, so the circulation is \(B(2\pi r)\), and \(B(2\pi r) = \mu_0 I\) gives \(B = \mu_0 I/2\pi r\) in one line, the same as the Biot–Savart integral of §28.5.

The Solenoid

A solenoid is a long, tightly wound coil, with \(n\) turns per unit length. Inside, the fields of all the turns add along the axis; outside, the contributions from the near and far sides of each turn nearly cancel, and for a long solenoid the outside field is close to zero.

Step 1 — choose the loop. A rectangle with one side of length \(\ell\) inside, parallel to the axis, and one side outside (Figure 28.12).

Step 2 — the circulation. Inside, \(\vec B\) runs along the side: \(B\ell\). Outside, \(B \approx 0\). On the two short sides, \(\vec B\) inside is perpendicular to the path, and outside it is zero: nothing.

\[\oint\vec B\cdot d\vec\ell = B\ell\]

Step 3 — the current through the loop. \(n\ell\) turns pass through it, each carrying \(I\): \(I_\text{enc} = n\ell I\).

Step 4 — Ampère’s law. \(B\ell = \mu_0 n\ell I\):

\[\boxed{\;B = \mu_0 nI \qquad \text{(inside a long solenoid)}\;}\]

The inside field does not depend on where you are inside, on the radius, or on the solenoid’s length; only on how tightly it is wound and the current. The solenoid is the magnetic parallel-plate capacitor.

Parallel-plate capacitor (Ch 25) Long solenoid
uniform \(E = \sigma/\varepsilon_0\) between the plates uniform \(B = \mu_0 nI\) inside
\(E \approx 0\) outside \(B \approx 0\) outside
energy density \(u_E = \tfrac12\varepsilon_0E^2\) energy density \(u_B = B^2/2\mu_0\) (Ch 29)

Example: The Field Inside a Solenoid

A solenoid has \(n\) turns per meter and carries current \(I\). Find the field inside for \(n = 1500\) turns/m and \(I = 4.00\) A.

Why it matters: the winding and the current are what an engineer chooses; the uniform field inside is what the device is for. This is the design equation for MRI magnets, relays and the electromagnets in a door lock.

Step 1 — symbols. \(B = \mu_0 nI\).

Step 2 — numbers.

\[\boxed{\;B = (4\pi\times10^{-7})(1500)(4.00) = 7.54\times10^{-3}\ \text{T} = 7.54\ \text{mT}\;}\]

About 150 times Earth’s field, from a few amperes. An MRI magnet reaches \(1.5\) T with superconducting wire, which carries hundreds of amperes with no resistance.

28.7 — Magnetic Flux and Gauss’s Law for Magnetism

Magnetic Flux

Chapter 31 defined the magnetic flux the same way Chapter 23 defined the electric flux. For a uniform field through a flat area \(A\) whose normal makes angle \(\theta\) with \(\vec B\),

\[\boxed{\;\Phi_B = \int\vec B\cdot d\vec A = BA\cos\theta \quad\text{(uniform } \vec B\text{)}, \qquad 1\ \text{Wb} = 1\ \text{T}\cdot\text{m}^2\;}\]

For a coil of \(N\) turns, the same flux passes through each turn, and the total \(N\Phi_B\) is called the flux linkage. Flux counts only the area where the field actually is.

Example: Flux Through a Solenoid, and Through a Coil Halfway In

(a) The solenoid of §28.6 (\(B = 7.54\) mT) has radius \(R = 2.50\) cm and length \(0.400\) m. Find the flux through one turn and the flux linkage of the whole solenoid. (b) A square loop of side \(\ell\) is pushed into a region of uniform field \(B\), perpendicular to the loop, so that a length \(x\) of it is inside (Figure 28.13). Find the flux through it for \(\ell = 20.0\) cm, \(B = 0.300\) T and \(x = 5.00\) cm.

Why it matters: the field and the geometry are known; the flux is the single number that Chapter 29’s law watches. When it changes, a current appears.

Step 1 — symbols. For the solenoid, the field fills the cross-section \(\pi R^2\) and there are \(N = n\ell_s\) turns. For the loop, only the area \(\ell x\) is in the field:

\[\Phi_\text{turn} = B\pi R^2, \qquad N\Phi = n\ell_s\,B\pi R^2; \qquad \Phi_\text{loop} = B\ell x\]

Step 2 — numbers. \(N = (1500)(0.400) = 600\) turns:

\[\boxed{\;\Phi_\text{turn} = (7.54\times10^{-3})\,\pi(0.0250)^2 = 14.8\ \mu\text{Wb}, \qquad N\Phi = (600)(14.8\ \mu\text{Wb}) = 8.88\ \text{mWb}\;}\] \[\boxed{\;\Phi_\text{loop} = (0.300)(0.200)(0.0500) = 3.00\times10^{-3}\ \text{Wb} = 3.00\ \text{mWb}\;}\]

The loop’s flux grows in proportion to how far it is in. If it moves at speed \(v\), \(x\) grows by \(v\) every second and the flux by \(B\ell v\) every second; Chapter 29 is about what that rate does.

Gauss’s Law for Magnetism

Every magnetic field line closes on itself. Wrap any closed surface around anything, and every line that enters must leave somewhere, so the net flux out is zero. This is Chapter 31’s law (2):

\[\boxed{\;\oint\vec B\cdot d\vec A = 0\;}\]

Its meaning is that there are no magnetic charges. Cut a bar magnet in half and you get two smaller magnets, each with a north and a south pole, never a lone pole. Compare Gauss’s law for \(\vec E\) (Chapter 23), where the flux out of a closed surface counts the charge inside. If a single magnetic pole is ever found, law (2) will need a right-hand side; searches since the 1930s have not found one.

28.8 — Summary

Key Concepts

  1. The field. \(\vec B\) pushes on moving charge only. Its direction is the line along which a moving charge feels no force; \(B = F_\text{max}/|q|v\), in teslas.
  2. The force on a charge is \(\vec F = q\vec v\times\vec B\), perpendicular to the motion. It does no work. A charge moving across a uniform field circles with \(r = mv/|q|B\) and a period \(2\pi m/|q|B\) that does not depend on its speed. Negative charges circle the other way.
  3. Crossed fields pass only \(v = E/B\) (the velocity selector). After one, a field alone sorts ions by mass (the mass spectrometer).
  4. The force on a wire is \(I\vec L\times\vec B\), the force on its carriers added up; \(N\) turns side by side give \(NILB\).
  5. A loop feels a torque \(\vec\tau = \vec\mu\times\vec B\) with \(\vec\mu = NIA\hat n\), and has energy \(U = -\vec\mu\cdot\vec B\), the electric-dipole results of Chapter 25 with new letters.
  6. Currents make the field. Biot–Savart gives \(\mu_0I/2\pi r\) beside a long wire and \(\mu_0I/2R\) at the center of a loop; fields add as vectors.
  7. Two currents push on each other with \(F/L = \mu_0I_1I_2/2\pi d\): parallel attract, antiparallel repel, equal and opposite even when the currents differ. This force fixed \(\mu_0\).
  8. Ampère’s law, the steady-current part of Chapter 31’s law (4), gives the wire in one line and \(B = \mu_0nI\) inside a solenoid.
  9. Flux and law (2). \(\Phi_B = BA\cos\theta\); through any closed surface the flux is zero, because there are no magnetic charges.

Looking Ahead

Every field in this chapter was steady: steady currents, fixed magnets, flux that never changed. Chapter 29 lets the flux change. Faraday found in 1831 that a changing magnetic flux through a loop drives a current around it with no battery anywhere: Chapter 31’s law (3), now from the experiment. A rod sliding across a field, a magnet pushed into a coil and the coil of §28.7 sliding into its field region all do it, and Lenz’s law fixes the direction of the current. Chapter 29 is the last chapter of the course. It also turns Faraday’s law on a coil’s own current to find the energy stored in a magnetic field, and it closes by setting all four field laws side by side, each now resting on a chapter of its own.
